task_row_model.query: How did Ottoman fiscal strain and administrative changes combine with local Greek institutions and Ottoman troop movements to enable the outbreak of the Greek War of Independence in 1821?

documents.content: An academic analysis of late Ottoman fiscal practice describes an acute revenue crisis in the early decades of the nineteenth century. The central treasury increasingly sold tax-collection rights by iltizam (tax-farming) and raised extraordinary levies to meet deficits, producing arrears and heavier peasant burdens in Anatolia and Rumelia. Earlier centralizing attempts such as Selim III's Nizam-i Cedid had already altered military and fiscal arrangements by undermining some local intermediaries' privileges. By the 1810s administrators resorted to more aggressive collection and auctions, which alienated rural notables and diminished the informal bargain that had stabilized Ottoman rule in many provinces.
documents.reasoning_trace: Identifies fiscal crisis, use of iltizam and extraordinary levies, and the erosion of local intermediaries' privileges; links to rural alienation needed for synthesis.

documents.content: A memoir-style account by a Greek armatolos recounts how local militias and klepht bands had long been embedded in Ottoman provincial order: armatoloi were licensed to collect local security revenue but, over time, their authority and stipends were reduced. The note emphasizes the formation of Filiki Eteria in Odessa in 1814 as a secret society that recruited members among the diaspora, local captains and klephts, storing arms and coordinating networks. When taxes rose and armatoloi privileges shrank, many of these local leaders kept arms and networks that Filiki organizers could mobilize for coordinated insurrection rather than isolated brigandage.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provides evidence that armatoloi/klephts retained arms and networks and that Filiki Eteria (founded 1814) recruited them—necessary to show local capacity for coordinated revolt.

documents.content: A contemporary consular report observed a strategic opening in 1820–1821 because Ottoman forces were distracted by the campaign against Ali Pasha of Ioannina. The report notes that the imperial government diverted troops and attention northward to suppress Ali's autonomous rule, which left reduced garrisons and a diminished rapid-response capacity in the Morea and other southern provinces. That military diversion, combined with existing local unrest, was explicitly cited as creating an opportunity for insurgent leaders to initiate synchronized uprisings in early 1821.
documents.reasoning_trace: Documents the diversion of Ottoman troops to confront Ali Pasha in 1820, reducing garrisons in the Morea and creating a military opening—crucial for timing of the uprising.

documents.content: A reference entry outlines the longue durée of Ottoman institutional change, from Janissary power to later nineteenth-century reforms, and includes speculative commentary on European philhellenism and missionary activity. It reprints statistical tables of tax revenue from the eighteenth century and sketches unrelated case studies of local revolts in Syria. The entry reiterates definitions of timar and iltizam and offers a broad, repetitive chronology of imperial reform that emphasizes continuities rather than the specific fiscal pressures and local networks in the 1810s.
documents.reasoning_trace: Contains background and tangential material (Janissaries, timar definitions, European philhellenism) not required for answering the focused causation question; serves as noise.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Mounting Ottoman fiscal strain—wider use of iltizam and extraordinary levies that raised peasant burdens and undermined local intermediaries—eroded armatoloi privileges. The secret Filiki Eteria (founded 1814) recruited armed klephts and diaspora networks, and the diversion of Ottoman troops to suppress Ali Pasha in 1820 reduced garrisons in the Morea. Together these factors created a coordinated, timely opening for the 1821 uprisings.
